title: The Fourier integral realizes the Plancherel transform on L1 intersect L2
statement: Over $\mathbf R,\mathbf C$ [def-weil-field], let $m\geq1$, and use Lebesgue measure. Let $L^2(\mathbf R^m;\mathbf C)$ be measurable square-integrable functions modulo almost-everywhere equality, with $\|u\|_2^2=\int|u|^2$. The Fourier integral on Schwartz functions (smooth functions whose derivatives decrease faster than every inverse polynomial), with kernel $e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}$, extends to a complex-linear isometric bijection $\mathcal F_2:L^2\to L^2$. Thus $\|\mathcal F_2u-\mathcal F_2v\|_2=\|u-v\|_2$ for all $u,v\in L^2$. If $u\in L^1\cap L^2$, the absolutely convergent integral $h(\xi)=\int e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}u(x)\,dx$ represents $\mathcal F_2u$ almost everywhere; in particular $h\in L^2$.

source.place: §2, p.3, Fourier transform and the s=0 case of (2.1); Lemma 2.7 proof, p.5, using the integral representatives of L2 Fourier transforms of fixed-support functions. The L1/L2 compatibility is made explicit as agent-stated supporting input. WANTED locally; read online https://www-fourier.univ-grenoble-alpes.fr/~demailly/analytic_geometry_2019/pseudodiff.pdf

proof.text: Apply [lem-sfb-l2-fourier-isometry-test-duality] to obtain the complex-linear isometric bijection $\mathcal F_2$ extending the specified Schwartz Fourier integral. Linearity and isometry give $\|\mathcal F_2u-\mathcal F_2v\|_2=\|\mathcal F_2(u-v)\|_2=\|u-v\|_2$. This proves the extension and distance clauses.

source.place: 50-55 and 99-105; linearity of the isometric equivalence.

proof.text: For $u\in L^1\cap L^2$, fix its measurable representative $u_0$ and a measurable representative $w$ of $\mathcal F_2u$. The identity $|e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\xi}u_0(x)|=|u_0(x)|$ proves absolute convergence of $h(\xi)$ at every $\xi$. Apply [lem-sfb-bilinear-fourier-moment-regularity] with $a=b=m$, $L(x,\xi)=x\cdot\xi$, $f=u_0$ and $r=0$: its only moment assumption is $u_0\in L^1$, so $h$ is continuous. Then [lem-sfb-continuous-local-integrability] on $U=\mathbf R^m$ makes $h$ locally integrable, while [lem-sfb-lp-local-integrability] at $p=2$ makes $w$ locally integrable.

Let $\psi$ be any real smooth compactly supported function, and put $\phi=\psi+i0$. By [lem-sfb-schwartz-test-inclusion-integrability], $\phi$ is Schwartz and integrable. Apply [lem-sfb-l1-bilinear-fourier-duality] with $f=u_0$, $q=\phi$ and $L(x,\xi)=x\cdot\xi$. Its two integrability hypotheses hold; symmetry of the dot product gives $J_{L^{\mathrm t}}\phi=\mathcal F\phi$. Thus $\int h\phi=\int u_0\mathcal F\phi$. The forward test identity of [lem-sfb-l2-fourier-isometry-test-duality] for $u,u_0,w,\phi$ gives $\int\phi w=\int(\mathcal F\phi)u_0$. Commuting complex products yields $\int\psi h=\int\psi w$.

source.place: 242-248 with the symmetric dot-product form, and LpSpace.lean:120-129 evaluated on the Schwartz test.

proof.text: Put $f=h-w$. Step 2 and $|h-w|\leq|h|+|w|$ show local integrability of $f$: intersect the two neighborhoods at each point. On the compact support of any test $\psi$, take a finite cover by such neighborhoods; boundedness of $\psi$ makes $\psi h$ and $\psi w$ integrable. Therefore step 3 and linearity of the integral give $\int\psi f=0$. Apply [lem-sfb-smooth-test-ae-separation] to $U=\mathbf R^m$ and $f$. Its openness, local integrability and all real smooth compact-test hypotheses have just been checked. Hence $h=w$ almost everywhere. Since $w$ represents $\mathcal F_2u$, the continuous function $h$ is square integrable and represents that same class, proving every remaining clause.
